clinician.final_diagnosis: CNS vasculopathy (versus CNS vasculitis) secondary to COVID-19 infection, presenting with acute ischemic stroke in posterior circulation
clinician.trajectory_summary: A 39-year-old previously fit and well male of Bangladeshi origin presented in March 2020 with a 9-day history of malaise, fever, and cough. On admission, he had severe type I respiratory failure (PO2 8.87, pCO2 3.5, pH 7.5, RR 60, O2 sat 85% on room air) with bilateral pneumonic infiltrates on chest X-ray. COVID-19 swab confirmed positive on day 3. He improved respiratory status by day 8 and was weaned to room air. However, on day 8, he developed acute focal neurological deficits including reduced Glasgow Coma Scale score, right-sided weakness, hemisensory loss, and diplopia. MRI brain with gadolinium revealed multiple acute ischemic infarctions in the territories of the left posterior inferior cerebellar artery (PICA) and bilateral posterior cerebral arteries (PCAs), affecting the left cerebellar hemisphere, cerebellar vermis, left thalami, and bilateral occipital lobes. MR angiography of the neck showed multifocal areas of narrowing and occlusions in both PCAs, especially the left PCA, initially suggestive of CNS vasculitis. Lumbar puncture was unremarkable except for mildly raised protein and was negative for HSV I/II, enterovirus RNA, and varicella zoster. He was treated with a 3-day course of methylprednisolone for possible CNS vasculitis. Within 2 weeks of admission to the neurorehabilitation unit, he showed rapid neurological improvement with residual mild to moderate cognitive impairments in executive and visuospatial functions and verbal fluency. The specialist consensus at the referring hospital favored CNS vasculopathy over vasculitis.

final.final_diagnosis: CNS vasculopathy (versus CNS vasculitis) secondary to COVID-19 infection, presenting with acute ischemic stroke in posterior circulation
final.trajectory_summary: A 39-year-old previously fit and well male of Bangladeshi origin presented in March 2020 with a 9-day history of malaise, fever, and cough. On admission, he had severe type I respiratory failure (PO2 8.87, pCO2 3.5, pH 7.5, RR 60, O2 sat 85% on room air) with bilateral pneumonic infiltrates on chest X-ray. COVID-19 swab confirmed positive on day 3. He improved respiratory status by day 8 and was weaned to room air. However, on day 8, he developed acute focal neurological deficits including reduced Glasgow Coma Scale score, right-sided weakness, hemisensory loss, and diplopia. MRI brain with gadolinium revealed multiple acute ischemic infarctions in the territories of the left posterior inferior cerebellar artery (PICA) and bilateral posterior cerebral arteries (PCAs), affecting the left cerebellar hemisphere, cerebellar vermis, left thalami, and bilateral occipital lobes. MR angiography of the neck showed multifocal areas of narrowing and occlusions in both PCAs, especially the left PCA, initially suggestive of CNS vasculitis. Lumbar puncture was unremarkable except for mildly raised protein and was negative for HSV I/II, enterovirus RNA, and varicella zoster. He was treated with a 3-day course of methylprednisolone for possible CNS vasculitis. Within 2 weeks of admission to the neurorehabilitation unit, he showed rapid neurological improvement with residual mild to moderate cognitive impairments in executive and visuospatial functions and verbal fluency. The specialist consensus at the referring hospital favored CNS vasculopathy over vasculitis.

ruled_out_or_less_likely_alternatives.basis: Although initially suspected based on MRA findings of multifocal vascular narrowing and occlusions, specialist consensus favored vasculopathy. Key distinguishing features include: (1) absence of CSF pleocytosis (LP described as unremarkable except mildly raised protein), (2) negative infectious workup (HSV, enterovirus, VZV negative), and (3) pattern of multifocal vascular involvement characteristic of COVID-19-associated endothelial dysfunction rather than inflammatory vasculitis
Lumbar puncture negative for HSV I/II, enterovirus RNA, and varicella zoster; CSF described as unremarkable except mildly raised protein with no documented pleocytosis

ruled_out_or_less_likely_alternatives.alternative: Primary respiratory failure as sole diagnosis
ruled_out_or_less_likely_alternatives.basis: Patient improved respiratory status by day 8 but then developed acute focal neurological deficits, indicating CNS involvement beyond respiratory pathology
